extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of classic essays, philosophy, and political theory (Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading of Montaigne's essay sections on custom, law, innovation, and obedience—normative and descriptive reflections on social practices and governance. Useful for literary, historical, or political-theory study of early modern attitudes toward custom and law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obey the laws of the place where one lives
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the rule of rules, the general law of laws, that every one observe those of the place wherein he lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne invokes Socrates as an example (refusing to escape by disobedience to magistrate). The maxim is presented as a fundamental social rule: private judgment should yield to established civil laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and conform to custom
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom seizes and ensnares us so that it is hardly in us to disengage ourselves from its gripe; whatever is off the hinges of custom is believed to be also off the hinges of reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Custom is inculcated from infancy and shapes what appears universal and genuine. Departing from custom provokes great reluctance and is often (unreasonably) perceived as irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be extremely cautious about altering established laws or customs
rubrics_metrics.description: There is danger and inconvenience in altering [a law]; government is a structure composed of divers parts... it is impossible to stir so much as one brick or stone, but the whole body will be sensible of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne gives institutional examples (Charondas' halter, Lacedaemonian insistence) and historical warnings: innovators often suffer and innovations can produce civil disorder, ruin, and corruption of manners.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislators/innovators must clearly discern defects and virtues before reforming
rubrics_metrics.description: Whosoever shall take upon him to choose and alter, usurps the authority of judging, and should look well about him, and make it his business to discern clearly the defect of what he would abolish, and the virtue of what he is about to introduce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private reason has private jurisdiction; one should not subject public institutions to a private fancy. The reformer bears special responsibility and risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: When laws are not understood, people still must obey them
rubrics_metrics.description: What can be more strange than to see a people obliged to obey laws they never understood... being neither written nor published in their own language, and of which they are of necessity to purchase both the interpretation and the use?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne criticizes systems where law is inaccessible or mediated by others (e.g., lawyers) but emphasizes the practical hold of such customs and legal regimes on people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer obedience and social peace to disruptive attempts at reform
rubrics_metrics.description: It argues a strange self-love and great presumption to be so fond of one's own opinions, that a public peace must be overthrown to establish them... to introduce so many inevitable mischiefs, as a civil war and the mutations of state consequent to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne judges that overthrowing public peace for one's opinions is poor stewardship; better to endure some imperfections than provoke broad social harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extraordinary necessities may justify temporary suspension or alteration of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortune sometimes presents us with a necessity so urgent, that 'tis requisite the laws should a little yield and give way... a legitimate proceeding is cold, heavy, and constrained, and not fit to make head against a headstrong and unbridled proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: He adduces examples (Agesilaus suspending laws for 24 hours, Alexander adjusting months) to show pragmatic flexibility in emergencies is permissible and sometimes prudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: The power of custom can substitute for reason and be morally binding
rubrics_metrics.description: The laws of conscience, which we pretend to be derived from nature, proceed from custom... the common fancies that we find in repute everywhere about us, and infused into our minds with the seed of our fathers, appear to be the most universal and genuine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customly-formed conscience renders many practices morally compelling; Montaigne stresses the psychological and social force of habit over abstract rational proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use clemency and mercy as prudent statecraft
rubrics_metrics.description: Clemency and forgiveness can transform conspirators into loyal subjects; Augustus forgave Cinna and later gained his friendship and loyalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne offers historical anecdotes (Augustus, the Duc de Guise) as examples where mercy produced political stability and eliminated further plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware imitation of innovations and their imitators
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventors do the greater mischief, the imitators are more vicious to follow examples of which they have felt and punished both the horror and the offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when an innovation is punished, imitation can spread the vice further; change begets precedents that trouble government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish between following forms (obedience) and attempting to change them (responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a vast difference betwixt the case of one who follows the forms and laws of his country, and of another who will undertake to regulate and change them; the first pleads simplicity, obedience, and example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who obey can claim innocence or misfortune; those who attempt reform 'usurp the authority of judging' and must answer for consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conform externally to social fashions while reserving inner freedom of judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: A wise man, within, ought to withdraw and retire his soul from the crowd, and there keep it at liberty and in power to judge freely of things; but as to externals, absolutely to follow and conform himself to the fashion of the time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne recommends pragmatic conformity in outward matters (dress, customs) to preserve social ease while maintaining private judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize corruption where justice becomes a commodity
rubrics_metrics.description: To see a nation where, by lawful custom, the office of a judge is bought and sold, where judgments are paid for with ready money, and where justice may legitimately be denied to him that has not wherewithal to pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne points out the perverse consequences—double laws of honour and justice, institutional division—of commodified justice as an anti-pattern.
